lessons.title: Nutrient Requirements of Sheep
lessons.body: Sheep need six key nutrients: water, energy, protein, minerals, vitamins, and fiber. Water is the most critical. A dry ewe drinks 4â8 liters per day; a lactating ewe can drink 10â15 liters. In hot African conditions, always provide clean water twice daily. Energy comes mainly from carbohydrates in pasture, hay, and grains. A dry ewe needs about 8â10% protein in her diet; a lactating ewe needs 14â16%. Growing lambs need 16â18% protein. Energy is measured in Total Digestible Nutrients (TDN). For maintenance, sheep need 50â60% TDN; for late pregnancy, 60â65%; for lactation, 65â70%. Fiber is essential for rumen health. At least 30% of the diet should be roughage like grass or hay. Minerals like calcium, phosphorus, and salt are needed in small amounts. Provide a free-choice mineral lick. Vitamins A, D, and E are important; green pasture provides these. In dry seasons, supplement with commercial sheep premix. A simple rule: watch body condition. A sheep with a body condition score of 2.5â3.5 (on a 5-point scale) is healthy. You can feel the spine and ribs but not see them. Adjust feed based on age, pregnancy, and lactation. Overfeeding concentrates can cause acidosis; underfeeding causes weight loss and poor reproduction. Always introduce new feeds gradually over 7â10 days. For African smallholders, use locally available feeds: maize bran, cottonseed cake, sunflower cake, and legume hays like lucerne or groundnut hay. Mix them to meet protein and energy needs. Clean water, good pasture, and a balanced mineral supplement will keep your sheep productive.

lessons.title: Pasture Management and Grazing
lessons.body: Good pasture is the cheapest feed for sheep. In Africa, common pasture grasses include Rhodes grass, Napier grass, star grass, and Kikuyu. Legumes like desmodium, stylo, and lucerne add protein. Rotational grazing is key. Divide your land into 4â6 paddocks using wire or live fences. Graze each paddock for 3â5 days, then rest it for 21â30 days. This prevents overgrazing and parasite buildup. Stocking rate: 1 sheep per 0.4â0.8 hectares on improved pasture; on poor rangeland, 1 per 2â4 hectares. In dry areas, reduce stocking. Always provide a mineral lick and clean water in each paddock. Avoid grazing wet pastures early in the morning when dew is heavyâthis reduces bloat and worm infection. For zero-grazing systems, cut and carry fresh grass and legumes daily. A mature ewe eats 2â4 kg of fresh forage per day. Mix grasses with legumes at a ratio of 70:30. Improve pasture by broadcasting seeds, applying manure or compost, and controlling weeds. In East Africa, many farmers use 'tumbukiza' pits for Napier grass to conserve moisture. During dry seasons, conserve excess grass as hay or silage. Rotational grazing also helps break the life cycle of internal parasites like Haemonchus contortus (barber's pole worm). If you see sheep with pale gums, bottle jaw, or diarrhea, move them to a clean paddock and deworm. Never let sheep graze too shortâleave 8â10 cm of grass height. Overgrazed pastures take longer to recover and invite weeds. For small flocks, a simple electric fence with two wires works well. Train sheep to electric fences by putting them in a small paddock for a few days. Always check fences for breaks. A well-managed pasture can carry 10â15 ewes per hectare in high-rainfall areas with good management.

lessons.title: Hay and Silage Production
lessons.body: Hay and silage are conserved feeds for dry seasons. Hay is dried grass or legumes; silage is fermented, high-moisture forage. To make good hay, cut grass at early flowering stage when protein is highest. Dry it in the sun for 2â3 days, turning it daily. Aim for 15â20% moistureâif you twist a handful, it should break, not drip. Store hay in a dry, ventilated shed on pallets to avoid mold. A ewe eats 1.5â2.5 kg of hay per day. Legume hays like lucerne or groundnut hay are richer in protein (15â20%) than grass hay (8â10%). For silage, chop fresh grass or maize stalks to 2â3 cm lengths. Pack tightly into a pit or silo, excluding air. Add molasses (2â3% of fresh weight) to improve fermentation. Cover with plastic sheet and soil. Silage is ready in 4â6 weeks. Good silage smells sweet and sour, not rotten. A ewe can eat 3â5 kg of silage per day. In Africa, maize silage is common. Harvest maize at dough stage (when kernels are soft but not dry). For smallholders, a 2x2x2 meter pit holds about 4 tons of silage, enough for 10 ewes for 3 months. Always test silage before feeding: if it is slimy, black, or smells like ammonia, discard it. Introduce silage gradually over a week. Hay and silage can be supplemented with concentrates. For example, feed 1 kg of hay plus 0.3 kg of maize bran to a lactating ewe. Store hay and silage away from rodents and moisture. In humid areas, use hay sheds with raised floors. Never feed moldy hayâit can cause listeriosis or abortion. Invest in a simple moisture meter or use the salt test: mix a handful of chopped hay with salt; if salt sticks, moisture is too high. Proper conservation saves money and keeps sheep healthy year-round.

lessons.title: Concentrate Feeding and Rations
lessons.body: Concentrates are energy- or protein-rich feeds like grains, oilseed cakes, and by-products. They are expensive, so use them strategically. Common African concentrates: maize, sorghum, millet, maize bran, wheat bran, cottonseed cake, sunflower cake, and soybean meal. A simple ration for a lactating ewe: 1.5 kg hay + 0.5 kg maize bran + 0.2 kg cottonseed cake + mineral lick. This provides about 16% protein and enough energy. For growing lambs, use 18% protein: 1 kg hay + 0.4 kg maize + 0.3 kg soybean meal. Always introduce concentrates slowly over 7â10 days to avoid acidosis. Start with 100 g per day and increase to full ration. Feed concentrates twice daily, after roughage. Never feed more than 0.5 kg of grain at one time per sheep. Mix feeds thoroughly. You can make a home-made ration: 50% maize bran, 30% cottonseed cake, 15% molasses, 5% mineral premix. This is a 14% protein mix. For dry ewes, 0.2â0.3 kg per day is enough. For rams during breeding, feed 0.5â0.8 kg of a 14% protein ration. Use a feed trough to prevent waste and contamination. Store concentrates in dry, rat-proof containers. Aflatoxin in moldy maize or cottonseed can kill sheep. Buy from reputable suppliers and check for mold. In East Africa, many farmers use 'sheep pellets' from companies like Unga or Pembe. If you mix your own, weigh ingredients with a simple scale. For 10 ewes, a weekly ration: 10 kg maize bran, 6 kg cottonseed cake, 3 kg molasses, 1 kg mineral premix. Mix well and feed 0.5 kg per ewe per day. Adjust based on body condition. If sheep get too fat, reduce concentrates. If they lose weight, increase. Always provide clean waterâconcentrates increase water needs. Avoid feeding urea to sheep unless properly mixed; urea toxicity is fatal. For smallholders, concentrate feeding is most cost-effective during late pregnancy and early lactation.

lessons.title: Mineral and Vitamin Supplements
lessons.body: Minerals and vitamins are needed in small amounts but are critical for health, growth, and reproduction. The most important minerals for sheep are salt (sodium and chlorine), calcium, phosphorus, selenium, copper, zinc, and cobalt. In many African soils, copper and selenium are deficient. However, sheep are sensitive to copper toxicityânever feed copper supplements meant for cattle. Provide a sheep-specific mineral lick free-choice. A good lick contains 15â20% salt, 8â10% calcium, 4â6% phosphorus, and traces of zinc, manganese, and selenium. You can buy commercial blocks or make your own: mix 5 kg salt, 2 kg dicalcium phosphate, 1 kg limestone, 0.5 kg trace mineral premix, and 0.5 kg molasses. Put in a wooden box with a roof. Sheep will lick 10â30 g per day. Vitamins A, D, and E are important. Green pasture provides beta-carotene (vitamin A precursor). In dry seasons, supplement with a vitamin premix or injectable vitamins. Vitamin E and selenium work together; a deficiency causes white muscle disease in lambs. In selenium-deficient areas (e.g., parts of Kenya, Tanzania, and South Africa), give ewes an injection of vitamin E/selenium 2â4 weeks before lambing. Vitamin B complex is synthesized in the rumen, so usually not needed. However, thiamine (B1) deficiency can occur with high-concentrate diets, causing polioencephalomalacia. If sheep show circling, head pressing, or blindness, give thiamine injection. Always provide clean waterâminerals need water for absorption. Salt blocks are not enough; they lack other minerals. Loose mineral mixes are better. Store minerals in a dry place. Do not mix minerals with concentrates unless you use a premix. Over-supplementation can be toxic, especially copper and selenium. Follow label directions. For organic or free-range systems, provide mineral licks year-round. Watch for signs of deficiency: poor growth, brittle bones, poor fertility, and white muscle disease. A simple blood test can confirm deficiencies, but visual signs and response to supplementation are often enough. Consult your local vet or extension officer for specific recommendations.

lessons.title: Feeding Different Age Groups
lessons.body: Feeding sheep by age and stage is key to success. Newborn lambs: colostrum within the first hour is critical. Colostrum provides antibodies and energy. If a lamb cannot suckle, tube-feed 50 ml per kg body weight of warm colostrum. For the first 3 days, lambs need 200â300 ml of milk per day, increasing to 1â1.5 liters by 4 weeks. From 1 week, offer creep feed: a mix of 18% protein pellets, maize bran, and molasses. Provide fresh water. Wean lambs at 8â12 weeks when they eat 200 g of creep feed per day. After weaning, feed a grower ration: 16% protein, 0.5â1 kg per day plus hay. Growing lambs need 0.2â0.4 kg of concentrate per day. For ewes: dry ewes need 0.2â0.3 kg concentrate plus pasture. In late pregnancy (last 6 weeks), increase to 0.5â0.7 kg of a 14% protein rationâthis prevents pregnancy toxemia. After lambing, lactating ewes need 0.8â1.2 kg of a 16% protein ration plus hay. Rams: during breeding, feed 0.5â0.8 kg of a 14% protein ration. In off-season, 0.2â0.3 kg. Always provide mineral licks and clean water. For orphan lambs, use cow milk replacer or goat milk; feed 4â5 times daily. Never feed cold milk. In Africa, many farmers use 'kienyeji' (local) sheepâthey are hardy but still need supplements during dry seasons. A simple rule: feed the best to the most productive. Lactating ewes and growing lambs get the most concentrates. Dry ewes and rams get less. Adjust based on body condition score. If a lamb is thin, increase feed. If a ewe is too fat, reduce. Introduce new feeds gradually. Always have roughage available. For sheep on zero-grazing, cut and carry fresh grass and legumes. For range sheep, provide supplements in troughs. Monitor weight monthly. A healthy lamb gains 150â200 g per day. If not, check for worms and adjust ration. Proper age-based feeding ensures high survival and fast growth.

quiz.q: What is the most critical nutrient for sheep?
quiz.explanation: Water is the most critical nutrient; sheep can die faster from lack of water than from lack of any other nutrient.

quiz.q: How much protein does a lactating ewe need in her diet?
quiz.explanation: Lactating ewes need 14-16% protein to support milk production.

quiz.q: What is the ideal body condition score for a healthy sheep?
quiz.explanation: A body condition score of 2.5-3.5 on a 5-point scale indicates healthy condition.

quiz.q: How long should you rest a paddock in rotational grazing?
quiz.explanation: Resting paddocks for 21-30 days allows grass to recover and reduces parasite larvae.

quiz.q: What is the recommended stocking rate on improved pasture?
quiz.explanation: On improved pasture, 1 sheep per 0.4-0.8 hectares is sustainable; poorer rangeland needs more land per sheep.

quiz.q: Which legume is commonly used to improve pasture protein?
quiz.explanation: Desmodium is a legume that adds protein to pastures and fixes nitrogen.

quiz.q: What is the ideal moisture content for hay?
quiz.explanation: Hay should be dried to 15-20% moisture to prevent mold and spoilage.

quiz.q: How long does silage take to ferment before feeding?
quiz.explanation: Silage is ready after 4-6 weeks of fermentation.

quiz.q: What should good silage smell like?
quiz.explanation: Good silage has a sweet and sour smell; a rotten or ammonia smell indicates spoilage.

quiz.q: Which feed is a good source of protein for sheep?
quiz.explanation: Cottonseed cake is a protein-rich concentrate (around 30-40% protein).

quiz.q: How should you introduce concentrates to sheep?
quiz.explanation: Gradual introduction over 7-10 days prevents acidosis and digestive upset.

quiz.q: What is the maximum amount of grain to feed at one time per sheep?
quiz.explanation: Never feed more than 0.5 kg of grain at once to avoid acidosis.

quiz.q: Which mineral are sheep particularly sensitive to in excess?
quiz.explanation: Sheep are sensitive to copper toxicity; never feed cattle mineral mixes to sheep.

quiz.q: What is a sign of selenium deficiency in lambs?
quiz.explanation: Selenium deficiency, often with vitamin E, causes white muscle disease in lambs.

quiz.q: How much mineral lick does a sheep consume per day?
quiz.explanation: Sheep typically lick 10-30 g of mineral supplement per day.

quiz.q: What is the first feed a newborn lamb must receive?
quiz.explanation: Colostrum within the first hour provides essential antibodies and energy.

quiz.q: At what age can lambs be weaned?
quiz.explanation: Lambs can be weaned at 8-12 weeks when they consume 200 g of creep feed per day.

quiz.q: How much concentrate should a lactating ewe receive daily?
quiz.explanation: Lactating ewes need 0.8-1.2 kg of a 16% protein concentrate daily.

quiz.q: What is pregnancy toxemia in ewes?
options: B) A condition from underfeeding in late pregnancy
quiz.explanation: Pregnancy toxemia occurs when ewes are underfed in late pregnancy, leading to ketosis.

quiz.q: Which vitamin is synthesized in the rumen and rarely needs supplementation?
quiz.explanation: Rumen microbes synthesize B vitamins, so supplementation is usually unnecessary.

quiz.q: What is the protein content of a good creep feed for lambs?
quiz.explanation: Creep feed should contain about 18% protein for growing lambs.

quiz.q: How much hay does a mature ewe eat per day?
quiz.explanation: A mature ewe consumes 1.5-2.5 kg of hay per day.

quiz.q: What is a sign of internal parasites in sheep?
quiz.explanation: Pale gums, bottle jaw, and diarrhea are signs of internal parasites like Haemonchus.

quiz.q: What is the best time to cut grass for hay?
quiz.explanation: Cutting at early flowering gives the best balance of yield and protein.

quiz.q: How much silage can a ewe eat per day?
quiz.explanation: A ewe can consume 3-5 kg of silage per day.

quiz.q: Which of these is a legume hay?
quiz.explanation: Lucerne (alfalfa) is a legume hay with high protein content.

quiz.q: What is the ideal ratio of grass to legumes in a pasture mix?
quiz.explanation: A 70:30 grass to legume ratio provides good protein and energy balance.

quiz.q: What is a simple test for hay moisture?
quiz.explanation: The salt test: mix salt with chopped hay; if salt sticks, moisture is too high.

quiz.q: How much water does a lactating ewe drink per day?
quiz.explanation: A lactating ewe can drink 10-15 liters of water per day, especially in hot weather.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of polioencephalomalacia in sheep?
quiz.explanation: Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, often from high-concentrate diets, causes polioencephalomalacia.
